details:
**Hou Yi shoots down nine of the ten suns**
In Chinese myth, ten suns (sons of the sun goddess Xihe) once rose together and scorched the earth. The archer Yi (Hou Yi) shot down nine of them, leaving one sun, and was rewarded with an elixir or pill of immortality.

**Chang'e, the moon goddess**
Yi's wife, who swallowed his pill of immortality and floated up to the moon, where she lives with a Jade Rabbit as her companion. She is honored during the Mid-Autumn Festival, when people eat mooncakes and admire the full moon.

**The Jade Emperor and the Great Race (zodiac)**
The Jade Emperor, ruler of heaven and head of the celestial bureaucracy, held a race among the animals to set the order of the twelve-year zodiac. The clever Rat rode across the river on the Ox's back and jumped ahead to finish first, followed by the Ox; the Pig came last. The cycle includes the Rabbit (2023) and the Dragon.

**The Cowherd and the Weaver Girl**
One of the "Four Great Folktales." The cowherd Niulang hides the clothes of seven bathing fairies and marries the weaver Zhinü, but her mother, the Queen Mother of the West, separates them with the Milky Way. Niulang follows her into the sky wearing his ox's hide, and the lovers became the stars Altair and Vega. Each year on the seventh day of the seventh month (Qixi), a bridge of magpies lets them meet.

**Pangu and the cosmic egg**
In the Chinese creation myth, the hairy, horned giant Pangu grew inside a black cosmic egg for 18,000 years, then broke it open and separated heaven (yang) from earth (yin). He pushed them apart, growing ten feet taller each day for another 18,000 years, and when he died his body became the features of the world.

**Nüwa**
A goddess with a serpent's lower body who created humanity by shaping people from yellow clay. After the sky was damaged, she repaired it with five-colored stones and cut the legs off a giant turtle to replace the pillars holding up the heavens.

**Gonggong smashes Mount Buzhou**
The water god Gonggong, angry after losing a battle, rammed his head into Mount Buzhou, one of the pillars holding up the sky. This tilted the heavens and earth and caused floods and disaster, which Nüwa then repaired.

**The Four Great Folktales**
Besides the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl, these are: Lady Meng Jiang, whose weeping for her husband, who died building it, made part of the Great Wall collapse; the Butterfly Lovers, Liang Shanbo and Zhu Yingtai, who turn into butterflies after death; and the Legend of the White Snake, about a snake spirit who gains magical powers and human form and falls in love with a man.

**Nian**
A beast that attacked villages at the start of the new year. It feared the color red, loud noises, and fire, which is said to explain the red decorations and firecrackers of Lunar New Year, a festival that also features dragon and lion dances.

**Sun Wukong, the Monkey King**
The mischievous monkey hero born from a stone, best known from the novel Journey to the West. He rebels against the Jade Emperor and wreaks havoc in heaven before being imprisoned under a mountain by the Buddha, and later escorts the monk Tang Sanzang to India.

**Gun and the swelling earth (xirang)**
When a great flood covered the land, the Four Mountains (the emperor Yao's advisers) chose Gun to stop it. He stole xirang, a self-expanding magical soil, from heaven to dam the waters, and was executed for it; his son Yu the Great later controlled the flood and founded the Xia dynasty.

**The Eight Immortals**
A group of Daoist immortals, each with a special emblem. One of them, Li Tieguai, is a lame, deformed beggar who walks with an iron crutch and carries a gourd (calabash) that releases vapor or holds medicine.

**Guardian lions**
Stone lion statues placed in pairs at the gates of palaces, temples, and homes to give protection. The male usually rests a paw on a ball (representing the world), and the female holds a cub.

**The Yellow Emperor and the Three Pure Ones**
The Yellow Emperor (Huangdi) is a legendary sage-ruler and culture hero regarded as the ancestor of the Chinese people. The Three Pure Ones are the highest deities of Daoism, the religion into which much of Chinese mythology was absorbed.
